directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Butterfly Japanese maple needs protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, which scorch its variegated leaves. Small, delicate, blue-green leaves are irregularly margined in creamy white, often blushed pink on new growth, giving the airy, upright canopy a light, fluttering appearance that inspired the cultivar's name, on a naturally narrow, columnar form well suited to a smaller garden or container where wider-spreading maples would be too large. Its fine-textured, variegated foliage provides season-long interest, turning soft yellow-pink in fall, and its upright habit makes it a good vertical accent for a shaded border or Japanese-style garden without the footprint of broader cultivars. Site out of hot afternoon sun and strong wind, which quickly scorch the delicate variegated leaf margins, and water during dry spells, especially for the first few years after planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Fernleaf Full Moon maple prefers cooler, more sheltered conditions than sun-tolerant Japanese maple cultivars.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Fernleaf Full Moon maple prefers cooler, more sheltered conditions than sun-tolerant Japanese maple cultivars. Deeply and finely dissected leaves, cut almost to the leaf base into slender, fern-like lobes, give this full moon maple relative a distinctly soft, feathery texture unlike the more classic star-shaped leaf of Japanese maple, turning an extraordinary blend of orange, red, and burgundy in fall that is often considered among the best of any maple's autumn display. Native to Japanese mountain forests, it is more cold-hardy but less heat-tolerant than many Japanese maple cultivars, performing best in cooler climates with protection from strong afternoon sun and wind. Provide consistent moisture and dappled shade, avoid hot, dry, or windy sites that stress the delicate foliage, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Golden Full Moon maple scorches in hot afternoon sun and needs protection from strong wind.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Golden Full Moon maple scorches in hot afternoon sun and needs protection from strong wind. Rounded, star-shaped leaves emerge a luminous chartreuse-gold in spring and hold their bright golden color through summer better than most yellow-leaved trees, glowing especially vividly in the dappled light of a shaded garden, before turning shades of orange and red in fall for a second seasonal color display. Slow-growing and long-lived, it develops a graceful, mounded, layered branching structure over the years that makes it a prized specimen tree for a shaded Japanese-style garden or woodland border, where its bright foliage color provides strong contrast against darker-leaved companions. Provide dappled shade and shelter from hot afternoon sun and drying wind, both of which scorch the delicate gold leaves, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist through summer.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Dragon Japanese maple holds its deep red color better in more sun than many other laceleaf cultivars, but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Dragon Japanese maple holds its deep red color better in more sun than many other laceleaf cultivars, but still benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Finely dissected, lacy, deep burgundy-red leaves cover a compact, mounding, weeping laceleaf form that holds its rich color from spring through summer better than many older red-leaved cultivars, which often fade toward green by midsummer, before finishing with a bright crimson fall display. Its dense, cascading, umbrella-like habit makes it a striking specimen for a container, rock garden, or the front of a shaded border, providing structure and color even without flowers. Provide afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, keep soil consistently moist but well drained, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge maple is exceptionally adaptable to poor soil, drought, pollution, and pruning, tolerating urban conditions better than most maples.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge maple is exceptionally adaptable to poor soil, drought, pollution, and pruning, tolerating urban conditions better than most maples. Small, rounded, dark green leaves with softly lobed margins cover a dense, tidy, small-to-medium tree that tolerates heavy pruning and shearing exceptionally well, making it a traditional European choice for clipped hedges and formal allees as much as a freestanding shade or street tree, turning a modest but pleasant yellow in fall. Native to Europe and western Asia, it is remarkably tolerant of poor, compacted, alkaline urban soils, drought, and air pollution, performing reliably in difficult street tree and parking lot planting sites where more particular maple species struggle. It needs little supplemental care once established beyond routine pruning if grown as a hedge, and its small mature size and dense branching make it a versatile shade tree for a smaller residential lot.
